correctness.rationale: Counting incidences gives MM^T=M^T M=qI+J and constant row and column sums q+1; each side has N=q^2+q+1 vertices. The two constant sectors and the paired zero-sum subspaces reduce both kernels to scalar ± blocks, with restricted singular value sqrt(q). For D_p the antisymmetric constant block starts at −1 at p=0 (off-diagonal convention) and is strictly decreasing because (q+1)log 2<q log 3; the lower paired block is strictly negative. The upper paired block changes sign at the unique root of (3/2)^p−(1/2)^p=1/sqrt(q), an increasing function from zero to infinity. At the root precisely N−1 mean-zero eigenvalues vanish; the centered Gram matrix has rank N there and 2N−1 strictly below. The zero diagonal and strictly positive off-diagonal squared distances give distinct points in the Gram realization. For the exponential kernel at t>0, the constant symmetric eigenvalue and upper paired block are positive; the two remaining displayed inequalities are exactly the other eigenvalue tests. Below or at the exponent threshold strict positivity for every t>0 follows from the Fourier representation of the Gaussian on the distinct embedded points. For p=1 and z=exp(−t), the two tested blocks factor as (1−z)(1−qz+q^2 z^2) and (1−z^2)(1−sqrt(q) z). The former is positive, and the latter gives exactly t=(log q)/2 as the positive boundary, with kernel rank N+1 there; t=0 is the separate rank-one case. For supercritical p the small-t derivative is negative on the positive distance block, while the large-t limit is I. Independent symbolic factorization and an exact shortest-path check on a cyclic Fano difference-set model gave boundary rank 8 and reproduced the stated q=2,p=2 example with the antisymmetric inequality failing alone.
residual_risks: The Fano calculation is bounded; scope for arbitrary existing and non-Desarguesian planes follows from the axiomatic proof. The two inequalities describe admissibility but do not enumerate bandwidth components for arbitrary supercritical p.

evidence: Voit covers PSD of every radial f(d) on a finite distance-regular graph via positive hypergroup spectral measure; Koohestani et al. give the distance-polynomial recurrence and the Q/Gibbs formulation. These supply spectral tests but do not evaluate or solve the projective-plane inequalities.

Murugan's determinant and nullspace criterion covers all constant-distance-row metrics; Sánchez computes the exponent for complete bipartite graphs of diameter two. The later symmetric-design finding covers both projective-plane negative-type and dimension phases as a special case, not the powered exponential covariance phase.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The association algebra, general PSD mechanism, and negative-type determinant test are prior machinery. The symmetric-design result genuinely covers the negative-type sector, but its PSD subject is the centered powered distance, not the exponential kernel.

evidence: A general radial theorem gives positivity from spectral weights. For the plane, writing A for adjacency, A2=A^2−(q+1)I and A3=(A^3−(2q+1)A)/(q+1), and evaluating at ±(q+1) and ±sqrt(q), gives an alternate route to the four blocks. The sign eliminations and the p=1 factorization then determine the two-parameter inequalities and the exact positive cutoff with rank. The calculation is specific to the diameter-three incidence algebra.

Knowing the exact negative-type region via the November results gives full Gaussian positivity for p≤p_q and failure at sufficiently small t above it, not the placement or nullity of the finite positive t boundary for p=1. The quadrangle theorem cannot be restricted by a parameter choice to these graphs.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: A method to calculate spectral positivity for any radial function is not an already explicit plane covariance phase. The new part credited is the evaluated parameter-space characterization and endpoint behavior for the natural family, not a new general association-scheme principle or a second claim to the covered negative-type results.

evidence: Q_z=(z^d) is exactly the ordinary-distance covariance with z=exp(−t). Tanaka determines when the entire interval [−1,1] is admissible, not the intermediate endpoint on planes; Obata studies graph gluing preserving Q positivity, in particular by square extensions, not this family with no four-cycles.

The q-distance matrix in Koolen et al. uses reciprocal geometric sums; at a geometric parameter s it is affinely related to the exponential matrix via K=J+(1/s−1)D_s. Its specific classical-parameter spectral conclusions are not an all-parameter admissibility result on a fixed projective plane.

Generalized roundness in the November 1 indexed record is equivalent to the frozen negative-type claim: same universal root and equality-space dimension. The snowflake metric d^(p/2) has exactly the same squared distances d^p.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: These equivalences identify strong prior comparisons rather than dismissing them by terminology. The negative-type equivalence is exact; neither full-interval Q-positivity nor a classification at a classical parameter identifies the positive boundary or rank for all t on the fixed graph.
searches: Q-matrices, Gibbs states, exponential distance kernels, generalized triangles and Heawood graph

evidence: The exact later projective-plane record gives sqrt(q)(3^p−1)=2^p, strictness below the boundary, and embedding ranks N and 2N−1. The symmetric-design record also explicitly includes that projective-plane phase.

The October 26 radial-cone record treats generalized quadrangles of diameter four; its ordinary-distance limit is (log(st))/2 with one-dimensional nullspace, not the plane's (log q)/2 with nullity N−1. No exact projective-plane powered exponential or positive-bandwidth rank entry was found in these checked sources.
exact_database_or_table.reasoning: An exact matching indexed threshold is credited even though the distinction between overlap and publication priority remains. Typical graph or adjacency spectrum tables do not themselves tabulate the bandwidth region or rank.
searches: Resultary: projective-plane metric, negative type, association schemes and Q-matrices

originality.rationale: The exact negative-type root and both Gram embedding ranks have material separately indexed coverage and are not credited here as a distinct contribution. The supported distinct component is the evaluated projective-plane powered-exponential covariance region, including its exact positive ordinary-distance threshold and covariance endpoint rank. The strongest primary sources provide the equivalent Gibbs/Q-matrix problem and general radial positivity machinery, not an evaluated projective-plane cutoff or this powered two-parameter region. The prior generalized-quadrangle classification is for a materially different graph and has a different phase and nullity.
residual_risks: The negative-type threshold and Gram rank are independently matched statements in the archive, without a provenance or priority conclusion. A historical exact projective-plane Q-matrix evaluation could still be hidden under design or association-scheme terminology. General radial PSD machinery is expressly credited; the assessment is only for the evaluated plane covariance claims.

value.rationale: For a natural infinite family of diameter-three finite geometries, the result tells exactly which powered radial exponential matrices can be covariance matrices, including examples where only one of two genuine obstructions fails. The simple ordinary-distance positive threshold and its large boundary nullspace quantify a sharp difference from all-bandwidth negative type and from the known quadrangle phase. The covariance classification and rank are useful even without counting the connected components of the powered parameter region.
residual_risks: This is not a classification of all distance-regular graphs, of the topology of every supercritical bandwidth slice, or of conditioning of nearly singular kernels.
